title: I keep panic closing my own algo mid trade. How do you actually deal with that fear?
author: Electronic_Tea_2948
selftext: So I recently put on a trade through my algo and then panicked halfway and shut it down manually. Again. I have basically always done this, jumped in and killed it the second it started going against me. For the past month I have been forcing myself to just let it run, but there is still this constant fear sitting in my chest the whole time, this voice telling me to close it before it gets worse. And most of the time, if I had just left it alone, it would have been fine. I am trying to figure out how to actually get past this. For those of you who trade systematically, how did you deal with the urge to interfere with your own system? Did the fear fade on its own with time and more data, or did you have to do something specific to get over it? And on the practical side, are there any setup or platform tricks that just take the decision out of my hands? Something that locks me out from closing early, or hides the live P&L so I stop babysitting every tick. Honestly I feel like I am the biggest risk to my own strategy right now and I want to fix that. Any advice appreciated.

comments.author: Pleasant_Thing_2874
comments.body:
The whole point of algo trading is to take emotion out of it.  If you don't have confidence in how it operates you're either risking too much money, you haven't had the algo prove itself in a more risk free environment or both.   Your algo should in theory also have kill switch rules so you know there's a max risk on your money and if it all goes to hell it'll stop on its own and then you can assess the damages as well as what went wrong.

If you're monitoring it live and sweating, you've missed a few steps.

comments.author: Fynca
comments.body: If you keep overriding it, either the size is too big or you don’t trust the testing yet. Reduce the size until the drawdowns feel boring, then judge the system over 50 trades, not one.

comments.author: Silver-Bullfrog9879
comments.body:
Is it playing with an amount of money that you can't afford to lose? Or can you not stand to lose at all? 

I'm never gonna give an algo anything more than fuck-it money. If it loses it all, no big deal.

comments.author: AttitudeGrouchy33
comments.body:
This is usually a sizing problem disguised as a psychology problem.

If you are watching every tick with your chest tight, the trade is too big for the amount of trust you actually have in the system. Doesn't matter what the backtest says. Your nervous system is voting with the close button.

What helped me: treat the algo like it is on probation, not like it has either passed or failed.

Tiny size. Pre-written kill rules. No discretionary closing unless one of those rules fires. Then review in batches, not trade by trade.

The thing I would log is not just PnL. Log every manual override too. What did the system say? What did you do? What happened if you had left it alone?

After 20-50 of those, you will probably learn something ugly and useful: either the algo is not trusted for a real reason, or you are the unstable part of the stack. Both are fixable, but only if you write it down.

comments.author: Middle-Following-367
comments.body: Your position sizes are too big if you’re having that type of visceral reaction.

comments.author: mojovski
comments.body:
thats very normal. I did that when I started too.  
You must train yourself to watch it and keep your hands of. invest the time rather in measuring the "success" of an algorithm. read books. it took me a few years until I found how to code successful algo metrics and now i let Ai build strategies with this metric.  
I would not have found this if I were watching the algos trading all the time.

comments.author: fomoz
comments.body: If you interfere, you ruin the expriment. Why bother building an algo bot at all?

comments.author: luisfernandez95
comments.body: Prueba bajar la cantidad en cada operación / o subir el stop cuando vas en beneficio
